{{Short description|Potential counterexample to the generalized Riemann hypothesis}}
In [[mathematics]], more specifically in the field of [[analytic number theory]], a '''Landau–Siegel zero''' or simply '''Siegel zero''', also known as an '''exceptional zero''',<ref name="seeiwa">See Iwaniec (2006).</ref> named after [[Edmund Landau]] and [[Carl Ludwig Siegel]], is a type of potential [[counterexample]] to the [[generalized Riemann hypothesis]], on the zeros of [[Dirichlet L-function]]s associated to [[quadratic number field]]s. Roughly speaking, these are possible zeros very near (in a quantifiable sense) to <math>s=1</math>.

==Motivation and definition==
The way in which Siegel zeros appear in the theory of Dirichlet L-functions is as potential exceptions to the [[Dirichlet L-function#Zeros|classical zero-free regions]], which can only occur when the L-function is associated to a real [[Dirichlet character]].

=== Real primitive Dirichlet characters ===

For an integer {{math|''q'' &ge; 1}}, a '''Dirichlet character''' modulo {{math|''q''}} is an [[arithmetic function]] <math display="inline">\chi\colon \mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}</math> satisfying the following properties:
* [[Completely multiplicative]]: <math display="inline">\chi(mn) = \chi(m)\chi(n)</math> for every {{math|''m''}}, {{math|''n''}};
* [[Periodic function|Periodic]]: <math display="inline">\chi(n+q) = \chi(n)</math> for every {{math|''n''}};
* Support: <math display="inline">\chi(n) = 0</math> [[if and only if]] <math>\mathrm{gcd}(n,q) > 1</math>.
That is, {{math|''&chi;''}} is the lifting of a [[homomorphism]] <math display="inline">\widetilde{\chi}:(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^{\times} \to \mathbb{C}^{*}</math>.

The '''trivial''' character is the character modulo 1, and the '''principal''' character modulo {{math|''q''}}, denoted <math display="inline">\chi_0~(\mathrm{mod}~q)</math>, is the lifting of the trivial homomorphism <math display="inline">(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\ni a \mapsto 1 \in \mathbb{C}^{*}</math>.

A character <math display="inline">\chi~(\mathrm{mod}~{q})</math> is called '''imprimitive''' if there exists some integer <math display="inline">d\neq q</math> with <math display="inline">d\mid q</math> such that the induced homomorphism <math display="inline">\widetilde{\chi}\colon (\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^{\times} \to \mathbb{C}^{*}</math> factors as
:<math>(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\twoheadrightarrow (\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z})^{\times} \xrightarrow{\widetilde{\chi'}} \mathbb{C}^{*}</math>
for some character <math display="inline">\chi'~(\mathrm{mod}~{d})</math>; otherwise, <math display="inline">\chi~(\mathrm{mod}~{q})</math> is called '''primitive'''.

A character <math display="inline">\chi</math> is '''real''' (or '''quadratic''') if it equals its [[complex conjugate]] <math>\overline{\chi}</math> (defined as <math>\overline{\chi}(n) := \overline{\chi(n)}</math>), or equivalently if <math display="inline">\chi^2 = \chi_0</math>. The ''real primitive Dirichlet characters'' are in one-to-one correspondence with the [[Kronecker symbol]]s <math display="inline">(D|\,\cdot\,): \mathbb{Z} \to \{-1,0,1\}</math> for <math display="inline">D\in\mathbb{Z}</math> a [[fundamental discriminant]] (i.e., the discriminant of a [[quadratic number field]]).<ref>See Satz 4, §5 of Zagier (1981).</ref> One way to define <math display="inline">(D|\,\cdot\,)</math> is as the completely multiplicative arithmetic function determined by (for {{math|''p''}} prime):
:<math>\bigg(\frac{D}{p}\bigg)=\begin{cases}1, &(p)\text{ splits in } \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D}), \\ -1, &(p)\text{ is inert } \cdots, \\ 0, &(p)\text{ ramifies } \cdots, \end{cases} \quad \bigg(\frac{D}{-1}\bigg) = \text{sign of } D.</math>
It is thus common to write <math display="inline">\chi_D := (D|\,\cdot\,)</math>, which are real primitive characters modulo <math display="inline">|D|</math>.

=== Classical zero-free regions ===
{{main|Dirichlet L-function#Zeros}}

The '''Dirichlet L-function''' associated to a character <math display="inline">\chi~(\mathrm{mod}~q)</math> is defined as the [[analytic continuation]] of the [[Dirichlet series]] <math display="inline">L(s,\chi) = \sum_{n\geq 1} \chi(n) n^{-s}</math> defined for <math display="inline">\mathrm{Re}(s)>1</math>, where ''s'' is a [[complex variable]]. For <math>\chi</math> non-principal, this continuation is [[Entire function|entire]]; otherwise it has a [[Zeros and poles|simple pole]] of [[Residue (complex analysis)|residue]] <math display="inline">\prod_{p\mid q}(1-p^{-1})</math> at {{math|''s'' {{=}} 1}} as its only singularity. For <math display="inline">\mathrm{Re}(s)>1</math>, Dirichlet L-functions can be expanded into an [[Euler product]] <math display="inline">L(s,\chi) = \prod_{p} (1 - \chi(p)p^{-s})^{-1}</math>, from where it follows that <math display="inline">L(s,\chi)</math> has no zeros in this region. The [[Prime number theorem#Prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions|prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions]] is equivalent (in a certain sense) to <math display="inline">L(1+it,\chi) \neq 0</math> (<math display="inline">\forall t\in\mathbb{R}</math>). Moreover, via the [[Dirichlet L-function#Functional equation|functional equation]], we can reflect these regions through <math display="inline">s\mapsto 1-s</math> to conclude that, with the exception of negative integers of same parity as {{math|''&chi;''}},<ref>{{math|''&chi;'' (mod ''q'')}} is ''even'' if {{math|''&chi;''(-1) {{=}} 1}}, and ''odd'' if {{math|''&chi;''(-1) {{=}} -1}}.</ref> all the other zeros of <math display="inline">L(s,\chi)</math> must lie inside <math>\{0<\mathrm{Re}(s)<1\}</math>. This region is called the '''critical strip''', and zeros in this region are called '''non-trivial zeros'''.

The classical theorem on zero-free regions (Grönwall,<ref>{{Cite journal | last=Grönwall | first=T. H. | author-link=Thomas Hakon Grönwall| year=1913 | journal=Rendiconti di Palermo | volume=35 | pages=145–159 | title=Sur les séries de Dirichlet correspondant à des charactères complexes | doi=10.1007/BF03015596 | s2cid=121161132 | language=fr}}</ref> Landau,<ref name="seeland">{{Cite journal | last=[[Edmund Landau|Landau]] | first=E. | year=1918 | journal=Göttinger Nachrichten | pages=285–295 | title=Über die Klassenzahl imaginär-quadratischer Zahlkörper | language=de}}</ref> Titchmarsh<ref>{{Cite journal | last=Titchmarsh | first=E. C. | author-link=Edward Charles Titchmarsh| year=1930 | journal=Rendiconti di Palermo | volume=54 | pages=414–429 | title=A divisor problem| doi=10.1007/BF03021203 | s2cid=119578445 }}</ref>) states that there exists an 
effectively computable real number <math display="inline">A>0</math> such that, writing <math>s=\sigma + it</math> for the complex variable, the function <math display="inline">L(s,\chi)</math> has no zeros in the region
:<math>\sigma > 1 - \frac{A}{\log q + \log (|t|+2)}</math>
if <math display="inline">\chi~(\mathrm{mod}~q)</math> is non-real. If <math display="inline">\chi</math> is real, then there is at most one zero in this region, which must necessarily be ''real'' and ''simple''. This possible zero is the so-called '''Siegel zero'''.

The [[generalized Riemann hypothesis]] (GRH) claims that for every <math display="inline">\chi~(\mathrm{mod}~q)</math>, all the non-trivial zeros of <math display="inline">L(s,\chi)</math> lie on the line <math display="inline">\mathrm{Re}(s)=\frac{1}{2}</math>.

=== Defining "Siegel zeros" ===
{{unsolved|mathematics|Is there <math display="inline">\delta >0</math> for which <math display="inline">L(\sigma,\chi_D)\neq 0</math> for every fundamental discriminant {{math|''D''}} provided <math display="inline">1-\frac{\delta}{\log|D|} < \sigma < 1 </math>?}}

The definition of Siegel zeros as presented ties it to the constant {{math|''A''}} in the zero-free region. This often makes it tricky to deal with these objects, since in many situations the particular value of the constant {{math|''A''}} is of little concern.<ref name="seeiwa" /> Hence, it is usual to work with more definite statements, either asserting or denying, the existence of an ''infinite'' family of such zeros, such as in:
* '''Conjecture''' ("no Siegel zeros"): ''If <math display="inline">\beta_D</math>'' denotes the largest real zero of <math display="inline">L(s,\chi_D)</math>, then <math>1-\beta_D \gg \frac{1}{\log|D|}.</math>

The possibility of existence or non-existence of Siegel zeros has a large impact in closely related subjects of number theory, with the "no Siegel zeros" conjecture serving as a weaker (although powerful, and sometimes fully sufficient) substitute for GRH (see below for an example involving Siegel–Tatsuzawa's Theorem and the [[idoneal number]] problem). An equivalent formulation of "no Siegel zeros" that does not reference zeros explicitly is the statement:
:<math>\frac{L'}{L}(1,\chi_D) = O(\log|D|).</math>
The equivalence can be deduced for example by using the zero-free regions and classical estimates for the number of non-trivial zeros of <math display="inline">L(s,\chi)</math> up to a certain height.<ref>See Chapter 16 of Davenport (1980).</ref>

== Landau–Siegel estimates ==

The first breakthrough in dealing with these zeros came from Landau, who showed that there exists an effectively computable constant <math>B>0</math> such that, for any <math display="inline">\chi_D</math> and <math display="inline">\chi_{D'}</math> real primitive characters to distinct moduli, if <math display="inline">\beta, \beta'</math> are real zeros of <math display="inline">L(s,\chi_D), L(s,\chi_{D'})</math> respectively, then
:<math>\min\{\beta,\beta'\} < 1- \frac{B}{\log|DD'|}.</math>
This is saying that, if Siegel zeros exist, then they cannot be too numerous. The way this is proved is via a 'twisting' argument, which lifts the problem to the [[Dedekind zeta function]] of the [[biquadratic field]] <math display="inline">\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D},\sqrt{D'})</math>. This technique is still largely applied in modern works.

This 'repelling effect' (see [[Deuring–Heilbronn phenomenon]]), after more careful analysis, led Landau to his 1936 theorem,<ref>{{Cite journal | last=Landau | first=E. |author-link= Edmund Landau| year=1936 | journal=[[Acta Arithmetica]] | pages=1–18 | title=Bemerkungen zum Heilbronnschen Satz | language=de}}</ref> which states that for every <math display="inline">\varepsilon > 0</math>, there is <math display="inline">C(\varepsilon)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}</math> such that, if <math display="inline">\beta</math> is a real zero of <math display="inline">L(s,\chi_D)</math>, then <math display="inline">\beta < 1 - C(\varepsilon)|D|^{-\frac{3}{8} - \varepsilon}</math>. However, in the same year, in the same issue of the same journal, Siegel<ref>{{Cite journal | last=Siegel | first=C. L. | year=1935 | journal=[[Acta Arithmetica]] | volume=1 | issue=1 | pages=83–86 | title=Über die Klassenzahl quadratischer Zahlkörper | doi=10.4064/aa-1-1-83-86 | language=de | url=http://pldml.icm.edu.pl/pldml/element/bwmeta1.element.bwnjournal-article-aav1i1p83bwm?q=bwmeta1.element.bwnjournal-number-aa-1935-1-1;6 | trans-title=On the class numbers of quadratic fields| doi-access=free }}</ref> directly improved this estimate to
:<math>\beta < 1 - C(\varepsilon)|D|^{-\varepsilon}.</math>
Both Landau's and Siegel's proofs provide no explicit way to calculate <math display="inline">C(\varepsilon)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}</math>, thus being instances of an [[Effective results in number theory|ineffective result]].

=== Siegel–Tatsuzawa theorem ===
In 1951, [[Tikao Tatsuzawa]] proved an 'almost' effective version of Siegel's theorem,<ref>{{Cite journal | last=Tatuzawa | first=T. | year=1951 | journal=Japanese Journal of Mathematics | volume=21 | pages=163–178 | title=On a theorem of Siegel| doi=10.4099/jjm1924.21.0_163 | doi-access=free }}</ref> showing that for any fixed <math display="inline">0 < \varepsilon < \frac{1}{11.2}</math>, if <math display="inline">|D| > e^{1/\varepsilon}</math> then
:<math>L(1,\chi_D) > 0.655\varepsilon|D|^{-\varepsilon}, </math>
''with the possible exception of at most one fundamental discriminant.'' Using the 'almost effectivity' of this result, [[Peter J. Weinberger|P. J. Weinberger]] (1973)<ref>{{Cite journal | last=Weinberger | first=P. J. | year=1973 | journal=Acta Arithmetica | volume=22 | pages=117–124 | title=Exponents of the class group of complex quadratic fields| issue=2 | doi=10.4064/aa-22-2-117-124 | doi-access=free }}</ref> showed that Euler's list of 65 [[idoneal number]]s is complete except for at most two elements.<ref>{{Cite journal| last=Kani | first=Ernst | year=2011 |title=Idoneal numbers and some generalizations | journal=Annales des Sciences Mathématiques du Québec | url=http://www.labmath.uqam.ca/~annales/volumes/35-2/PDF/197-227.pdf |volume=35 |number=2 |at=Remark 24}}</ref>

== Relation to quadratic fields ==
Siegel zeros often appear as more than an artificial issue in the argument for deducing zero-free regions, since zero-free region estimates enjoy deep connections to the arithmetic of quadratic fields. For instance, the identity <math display="inline">\zeta_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D})}(s) = \zeta(s) L(s,\chi_D)</math> can be interpreted as an analytic formulation of [[quadratic reciprocity]] (see [[Artin reciprocity law#Statement in terms of L-functions|Artin reciprocity law §Statement in terms of L-functions]]). The precise relation between the distribution of zeros near {{math|''s'' {{=}} 1}} and arithmetic comes from [[Class number formula#Dirichlet class number formula|Dirichlet's class number formula]]:
:<math> L(1,\chi_D) =
\begin{cases} \dfrac{2 \pi}{w_D \sqrt{|D|}}  \, h(D), &\text{if } D < 0 \\[.5em]
\dfrac{\log\varepsilon_D}{\sqrt{D}}\, h(D), &\text{if } D > 0,
\end{cases}</math>
where:
* <math display="inline">h(D)</math> is the [[Ideal class group#Properties|ideal class number]] of <math display="inline">\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D})</math>;
* <math display="inline">w_D</math> is the number of [[roots of unity]] in <math display="inline">\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D})</math> ({{math|''D'' &lt; 0}});
* <math display="inline">\varepsilon_D</math> is the [[Fundamental unit (number theory)|fundamental unit]] of <math display="inline">\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D})</math> ({{math|''D'' &gt; 0}}).
This way, estimates for the largest real zero of <math display="inline">L(s,\chi_D)</math> can be translated into estimates for <math display="inline">L(1,\chi_D)</math> (via, for example, the fact that <math display="inline">|L'(\sigma,\chi)| = O(\log^2 q)</math> for <math display="inline">1-\frac{1}{\log q} \leq \sigma \leq 1</math>),<ref>See (11) in Chapter 14 of Davenport (1980).</ref> which in turn become estimates for <math display="inline">h(D)</math>. Classical works in the subject treat these three quantities essentially interchangeably, although the case {{math|''D'' &gt; 0}} brings additional complications related to the fundamental unit.

=== Siegel zeros as 'quadratic phenomena' ===
There is a sense in which the difficulty associated to the phenomenon of Siegel zeros in general is entirely restricted to quadratic extensions. It is a consequence of the [[Kronecker–Weber theorem]], for example, that the [[Dedekind zeta function]] <math display="inline">\zeta_{K}(s) = \sum_{I\subseteq \mathfrak{O}_K} [\mathfrak{O}_K: I]^{-s}</math> of an [[Abelian extension|abelian number field]] <math display="inline">K/\mathbb{Q}</math> can be written as a product of Dirichlet L-functions.<ref>Theorem 10.5.25 in {{Cite book|last=Cohen|first=H.|author-link=Henri Cohen (number theorist)|url=https://www.springer.com/gp/book/9780387498935|title=Number Theory: Volume II: Analytic and Modern Tools|date=2007|publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer-Verlag]]|isbn=978-0-387-49893-5|series=Graduate Texts in Mathematics, Number Theory|location=New York|language=en}}.</ref> Thus, if <math display="inline">\zeta_{K}(s)</math> has a Siegel zero, there must be some subfield <math display="inline">F\subseteq K</math> with <math display="inline">[F:\mathbb{Q}] = 2</math> such that <math display="inline">\zeta_{F}(s)</math> has a Siegel zero.

While for the non-abelian case <math display="inline">\zeta_{K}(s)</math> can only be factored into more complicated [[Artin L-function]]s, the same is true:

* '''Theorem''' ([[Harold Stark|Stark]], 1974)'''.'''<ref>Lemma 8 in {{Cite journal|last=Stark|first=H. M.|date=1974-06-01|title=Some effective cases of the Brauer-Siegel Theorem|journal=Inventiones Mathematicae|language=en|volume=23|issue=2|pages=135–152|doi=10.1007/BF01405166|bibcode=1974InMat..23..135S |s2cid=119482000|issn=1432-1297}}</ref> Let <math display="inline">K/\mathbb{Q}</math> be a number field of degree {{math|''n'' &gt; 1}}. There is a constant <math display="inline">c(n)</math> (<math display="inline">= 4</math> if <math display="inline">K/\mathbb{Q}</math> is normal, <math display="inline">= 4n!</math> otherwise) such that, if there is a real <math display="inline">\beta</math> in the range
:<math display>1 - \frac{c(n)}{\log|\Delta_K|} \leq \beta < 1</math>
:with <math display="inline">\zeta_K(\beta) = 0</math>, then there is a quadratic subfield <math display="inline">F\subseteq K</math> such that <math display="inline">\zeta_{F}(\beta)=0</math>. Here, <math display="inline">\Delta_K</math> is the [[Discriminant of an algebraic number field|field discriminant]] of the extension <math display="inline">K/\mathbb{Q}</math>.

== "No Siegel zeros" for ''D'' < 0 ==
When dealing with quadratic fields, the case <math display="inline">D>0</math> tends to be elusive due to the behaviour of the fundamental unit. Thus, it is common to treat the cases <math display="inline">D<0</math> and <math display="inline">D>0</math> separately. Much more is known for the negative discriminant case:

=== Lower bounds for ''h''(''D'') ===
In 1918, [[Erich Hecke]] showed that "no Siegel zeros" for <math display="inline">D<0</math> implies that <math display="inline">h(D) \gg \sqrt{|D|}(\log|D|)^{-1}</math><ref name="seeland"/> (see [[Class number problem]] for comparison). This can be extended to an equivalence, as it is a consequence of Theorem 3 in [[Andrew Granville|Granville]]–[[Harold Stark|Stark]] (2000):<ref name="seegrst">{{Cite journal|last1=Granville|first1=A.|last2=Stark|first2=H.M.|date=2000-03-01|title=ABC implies no "Siegel zeros" for L-functions of characters with negative discriminant|journal=Inventiones Mathematicae|language=en|volume=139|issue=3|pages=509–523|doi=10.1007/s002229900036|bibcode=2000InMat.139..509G |s2cid=6901166|issn=1432-1297}}</ref>
:<math>\text{“No Siegel zeros” for } D<0 \quad\iff\quad h(D) \gg \frac{\sqrt{|D|}}{\log|D|}\sum_{(a,b,c)} \frac{1}{a}, </math>
where the summation runs over the [[Binary quadratic form#Reduction and class numbers|reduced]] [[binary quadratic form]]s <math display="inline">ax^2 + bxy + cy^2</math> of discriminant <math display="inline">D</math>. Using this, Granville and Stark showed that a certain uniform formulation of the [[abc conjecture]] for number fields implies "no Siegel zeros" for negative discriminants.

In 1976, [[Dorian Goldfeld]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Goldfeld|first=Dorian M.|author-link=Dorian Goldfeld|year=1976|title=The class number of quadratic fields and the conjectures of Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer|url=http://www.numdam.org/item/?id=ASNSP_1976_4_3_4_623_0|journal=Annali della Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa - Classe di Scienze|language=fr|volume=3|issue=4|pages=623–663}}</ref> proved the following unconditional, effective lower bound for <math display="inline">h(D)</math>:
:<math>h(D) \gg \prod_{p\mid D} \bigg(1-\frac{2\sqrt{p}}{p+1}\bigg)\, \log|D|. </math>

=== Complex multiplication ===
Another equivalence for "no Siegel zeros" for <math display="inline">D<0</math> can be given in terms of [[Upper and lower bounds|upper bounds]] for [[Height function|heights]] of [[Complex multiplication#Singular moduli|singular moduli]]:
:<math>h(j(\tau_D)) \ll \log|D|, </math>
where:
* <math display="inline">h</math> is the absolute [[Height function#Height functions in Diophantine geometry|logarithmic naïve height]] for number fields;
* <math display="inline">j</math> is the [[j-invariant|j-invariant function]];
* <math display="inline">\tau_D := (D+\sqrt{D})/2</math>.
The number <math display="inline">j(\tau_D)</math> generates the [[Hilbert class field]] of <math display="inline">\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D})</math>, which is its maximal unramified abelian extension.<ref>Theorem II.4.1 in {{Citation | last=Silverman | first=Joseph H. | author-link=Joseph H. Silverman | title=Advanced topics in the arithmetic of elliptic curves | year=1994 | publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | location=New York | isbn=978-0-387-94325-1 | series=[[Graduate Texts in Mathematics]] | volume=151}}.</ref> This equivalence is a direct consequence of the results in Granville–Stark (2000),<ref name="seegrst"/> and can be seen in C. Táfula (2019).<ref>{{cite journal|author=Táfula, C.|title=On Landau–Siegel zeros and heights of singular moduli|journal=[[Acta Arithmetica]]|year=2021|volume=201|pages=1–28|doi=10.4064/aa191118-18-5|arxiv=1911.07215|s2cid=208138549}}</ref>

A precise relation between heights and values of L-functions was obtained by [[Pierre Colmez]] (1993,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Colmez|first=Pierre|author-link=Pierre Colmez|year=1993|title=Periodes des Variétés Abéliennes à Multiplication Complexe|journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]]|volume=138|issue=3|pages=625–683|doi=10.2307/2946559|jstor=2946559|issn=0003-486X}}</ref> 1998<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Colmez|first=Pierre|date=1998-05-01|title=Sur la hauteur de Faltings des variétés abéliennes à multiplication complexe|journal=[[Compositio Mathematica]]|language=en|volume=111|issue=3|pages=359–369 | url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/compositio-mathematica/article/sur-la-hauteur-de-faltings-des-varietes-abeliennes-a-multiplication-complexe/AE329EE32B7B61AB1A95B308EEC4B5B6|doi=10.1023/A:1000390105495 |issn=1570-5846|url-access=subscription}}</ref>), who showed that, for an elliptic curve <math display="inline">E_D/\mathbb{C}</math> with [[complex multiplication]] by <math display="inline">\mathbb{Z}[\tau_D]</math>, we have
:<math> -2 h_{\mathrm{Fal}}(E_D) - \frac{1}{2} \log|D| = \frac{L'}{L}(0,\chi_D) + \log 2\pi, </math>
where <math display="inline">h_{\mathrm{Fal}}</math> denotes the [[Height function#Height functions in Diophantine geometry|Faltings height]].<ref>See the diagram in subsection 0.6 of Colmez (1993). There is small typo in the upper right corner of this diagram, that should instead read "<math display="inline">-2 h_{\mathrm{Fal}}(X) - \frac{1}{2}\log D</math>".</ref> Using the identities <math display="inline">h_{\mathrm{Fal}}(E_D) = \frac{1}{12}h(j(\tau_D)) + O(\log h(j(\tau_D)))</math><ref>Proposition 2.1, Chapter X of {{Cite book|url=https://www.springer.com/gp/book/9780387963112|title=Arithmetic Geometry|date=1986|publisher=Springer-Verlag|isbn=978-0-387-96311-2|editor-last=Cornell|editor-first=G.|location=New York|language=en|editor-last2=Silverman|editor-first2=J. H.}}</ref> and <math display="inline">\frac{L'}{L}(1,\chi_D) = -\frac{L'}{L}(0,\chi_D) - \log|D| + \log 2\pi + \gamma</math>,<ref>Consequence of the [[Dirichlet L-function#Functional equation|functional equation]], where {{math|&gamma; {{=}} 0.57721...}} is the [[Euler–Mascheroni constant]].</ref> Colmez' theorem also provides a proof for the equivalence above.

== Consequences of Siegel zeros existing ==
Although the [[generalized Riemann hypothesis]] is expected to be true, since the "no Siegel zeros" conjecture remains open, it is interesting to study what consequences such severe counterexamples to the GRH would imply. Another reason to study this possibility is that the proof of certain unconditional theorems require the division into two cases: first a proof assuming no Siegel zeros exist, then another assuming Siegel zeros do exist. A classical theorem of this type is [[Linnik's theorem]] on the smallest [[Primes in arithmetic progression|prime in an arithmetic progression]].

The following are some examples of facts that follow from the existence of Siegel zeros.

=== Infinitude of twin primes ===
{{main|Twin prime}}

A striking result in this direction is [[Roger Heath-Brown]]'s 1983 result<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Heath-Brown|first=D. R.|author-link=Roger Heath-Brown|date=1983-09-01|title=Prime Twins and Siegel Zeros|url=https://academic.oup.com/plms/article/s3-47/2/193/1524169|journal=[[London Mathematical Society|Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society]]|language=en|volume=s3-47|issue=2|pages=193–224|doi=10.1112/plms/s3-47.2.193|issn=0024-6115|url-access=subscription}}</ref> which, following [[Terence Tao]],<ref>{{Cite web|date=2015-08-27|title=Heath-Brown's theorem on prime twins and Siegel zeroes|url=https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2015/08/26/heath-browns-theorem-on-prime-twins-and-siegel-zeroes/|access-date=2021-03-13|website=What's new|language=en}}</ref> can be stated as follows:
* '''Theorem''' (Heath-Brown, 1983)'''.''' At least one of the following is true: ''(1)'' There are no Siegel zeros. (''2)'' There are infinitely many [[twin prime]]s.

=== Parity problem ===
{{main|Parity problem (sieve theory)}}

The parity problem in [[sieve theory]] roughly refers to the fact that sieving arguments are, generally speaking, unable to tell if an integer has an even or odd number of prime divisors. This leads to many upper bounds in sieve estimates, such as the one from the [[linear sieve]]<ref>See Chapter 9 of {{Cite book|last=Nathanson|first=Melvyn B.|url=https://www.springer.com/gp/book/9780387946566|title=Additive Number Theory The Classical Bases|date=1996|publisher=Springer-Verlag|isbn=978-0-387-94656-6|series=Graduate Texts in Mathematics|location=New York|language=en}}</ref> being off by a factor of 2 from the expected value. In 2020, [[Andrew Granville|Granville]]<ref>{{cite arXiv|author=Granville, A.|title=Sieving intervals and Siegel zeros|year=2020|class=math.NT|eprint=2010.01211}}</ref> showed that under the assumption of the existence of Siegel zeros, the general upper bounds for the problem of sieving intervals are optimal, meaning that the extra factor of 2 coming from the parity phenomenon would thus not be an artificial limitation of the method.
